utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the opportunity to put the following on the record. The Chamber recalls the Prosecution requests to use common charts with upcoming witness, John Clark, and witness RM016DD and the Chamber hereby grants the same. Then a follow-up to the decision of the 14th Rule 92 bis motion. Witness RM37's statements and associated exhibits were admitted on the 28th of June of this year on the condition that the Prosecution provide the required attestation pursuant to Rule 92 bis B. The Chamber has reviewed the attestation in the meantime, and hereby confirms admission of P2227 up to and including P2229. The last item I'd like to deal with is a short corrigendum. And it's a follow-up to a decision on the Prosecution's 22nd motion Rule 92 bis. The motion was filed on the 23rd of August of this year, and one of the admitted transcript portions in the Chamber's decision for Witness RM001 appears as 6422, lines 13 to 15, the decision should read, lines 13 to 25. Furthermore all references in the decision to Rule 65 ter numbers 7701A and 7701B should be understood as referring to 6701A and 6701B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, when I said that the 22nd motion Rule 92 bis motion was filed on the 23rd of August I made a mistake because it was the decision which was filed on that day and it's a correction to that decision. Good morning, Mr. Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apologies for continuing with a procedural matter when you entered the courtroom, but we'll now immediately start. Mr. Lukic, if you're ready, and after I have reminded Mr. Milovanovic that he is still bound by the solemn declaration he has given at the beginning of his testimony, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we call up in e-court P2219.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, you were shown this document. As we could see, the translation is wrong. At this time, I should like to ask that a translation be revised. We -- I think we do know the correct translation of item 2 of page 17005, line 19. Therefore, on that page our -- transcript can we find the correct translation. This is my question for you, General. My learned friend Groome tied the issue of this document with the incident at Dobrinja and the incident at Markale that we've referred to as Markale I of February 1994, but I'll not be asking you about that specifically because this is a matter for experts in ballistics to deal with. I'll ask you this: Were you aware of the fact that the Muslim authorities opened fire at their own population in order to gain the sympathy of western countries and make NATO proceed with air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were stories to that effect all around, especially after the incident of 27 May 1992, when those citizens lining up for bread or water in Vase Miskina Street were killed. The Serbs were accused. Now, the investigation into who was responsible was discontinued because a Muslim delegation abandoned talks for, I believe, Cutileiro Plan 2. The negotiations fell through. This was especially much talked about after Markale I. I'm not that familiar with the incident at Dobrinja, though I am familiar with Markale I. I had several talks with the Chief of Staff of UNPROFOR, General Ramsey. On that first evening, blame was attached to the Serbs right away, and this was aired. However, over the course of the following several days, it turned out that it wasn't the sort of shell that he was mentioning and then some other issues surfaced as well. So the incident which was initially attributed to the Serb -- was open to doubt. As for the Muslims, well, it was common knowledge that the Muslims waged wars amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have answered my next question, in part. It is of a more general nature. Was it during and before the international conference and in the course of a visit of a foreign delegation the case that civilians would be killed on a massive scale in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can state quite responsibly that such incidents where Muslim civilians would be killed on a massive scale would take place precisely at the time or prior to certain negotiations. Or, if the Muslim side, and this was something that they always aspired toward, prompted NATO to engage in air-strikes against the Serbs. So they would be provoking the Serbs, who would then respond, and that's how it would end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, no time-frame, no specifics. Just general statements which will not assist the Chamber. Whereas, the Chamber would be interested in having detailed information about such events. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, my question was general, and your answer was general, too, then. This is my next question: Do you know of any specific, say, around Markale I, what conference was in course at the time, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which conference it was specifically. It was about Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I don't know the specific topic. General Mladic and Karadzic were both present. I think it was an attempt to stop the war in Sarajevo. It had to do with a demilitarisation of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Following the incident at Markale, pressure was brought to bear upon the Serbs to withdraw their armaments; right? And I mean around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following Markale, NATO issued an ultimatum that we should withdraw our artillery away from Sarajevo. At first, it was 30 kilometres; and then, as I said, in the agreement, 20 kilometres were referred to. The Serbs were faced with a choice: Either to withdraw their artillery, i.e., to fulfil the ultimatum; or to refuse to implement the ultimatum and suffer bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were any obligations imposed upon the Muslim side in situations such as this one? Say, post-Markale, in terms of withdrawal of weaponry. We heard that the Serbs were supposed to withdraw their weapons away from Sarajevo. Was something of the nature imposed upon the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that in the ultimatum NATO requested something of the sort from the Muslims but I do know that commander of UNPROFOR Bosnia-Herzegovina, General Michael Rose, placed a similar requirement upon the Muslims, that they should withdraw their weaponry. Our counter-request was that, since we were more powerful and withdrawing our artillery away from Sarajevo, the Muslims should withdraw elements of their infantry from their positions into barracks, because their infantry was powerful. The negotiations on the 9th of February arranged this, but this was never effected. We withdrew our artillery, but the entire Muslim corps continued to occupy their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were shown two documents: P2200 and P2221. The question that followed had to do with fuel air-bombs. Your -- you said that you weren't familiar with those. I'll explain to you now what it was that you were shown, in fact. This sort of bombs used the blast effect to kill personnel rather than damage buildings. Fuel air-bombs were used in Vietnam when the Americans called them a specific name because they were used for the destruction of forests and vegetation. They were called Daisy Mower. Did the Serb army possess such bombs, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said over the past days that I only heard of these fuel air-bombs in connection with my studies of the Vietnam war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were next asked to describe the launchers of aerial bombs. They were referred to as "skalamerija". The Greek word "skelanos" means distorted. In our language, in slang it's a term that is used for any sort of item that -- whose purpose isn't really known or to what use it can be put. Any sort of contraption, really. Would this term of "skalamerija" be an official term that is used?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just seems I let the previous question go. But now this one question seems -- again, Mr. Lukic seems to be testifying or providing evidence which I'm not sure it's the most appropriate way to get this before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That came to my mind as well, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps the Chamber might permit exceptionally the interpreters just to explain to us what the word "skalamerija" means in English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It means "contraption."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it's usually in this courtroom that we sometimes have citations from vocabulary, or from -- from books, how they are explained. So I wanted to ask General whether it's official name for this weapon or some -- it's something -- what he used to name this weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ask questions of fact, Mr. -- yes, let me see. Whether it's the official name of this weapon is one. But I'm just looking at the -- what the witness said about this name at all. Because -- let me check. I'm looking at page 17015. Do you know what weapons Mr. Lukic is talking about? And did you have a name for that weapon he refers to? What name did you use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Over the past day, I referred to this "skalamerija," "the contraption". In Serbian it means that it's an item that was put together in a makeshift way, looks quite cumbersome, but is useful. Colonel Rajko Balac, chief of artillery, and I referred to it as "skalamerija" and it was called "skalamerija 94," in fact. It was no official name for it. An official name for it would be "aerial bomb launcher." I wasn't aware of any code-name for it, M94, or anything of that kind. As for the piece itself, I only saw a model of it. I never saw it in real life, in transport, or in combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The reason why I was a bit confused, Mr. Lukic, is because the witness used the name "skalamerija" himself previously. So apparently it's not an official name. I still am a bit lost where we are going at this moment. But put clear questions to the witness, and you might get me on track again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will move on. I had not dwell on this -- this topic anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I'd like to ask you questions about President Karadzic now. Did it so happen in the war-time years in Bosnia-Herzegovina that you received orders directly from President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it's my recollection that the witness said that this happened now and then and that he then told Mr. Karadzic there was no use of doing it because he would always first verify with Mr. Mladic. So, therefore, I do not know if there's anything in addition to that you'd like to know. Ask the witness, but he has told us quite a bit about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wanted to specifically ask you about 1995, when problems emerge in the western front, threatening entire municipalities in Republika Srpska. Can you describe the situation in more detail for us, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you still with -- receiving orders from Mr. Karadzic directly?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's not clear from your question. Could you tell us about direct orders you received in the -- at the western front in approximately 1995, receiving direct orders from Mr. Karadzic? Did you receive such orders? First question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did receive such orders in July and August 1995 up until the time when General Mladic arrived on the western front which was sometime in early August 1995. He attended a meeting of the Supreme Command in Drvar and stayed by my side until the end. However, despite the fact that General Mladic was present, President Karadzic visited with me at the IKM of the Main Staff and tried to give me orders. But I did tell him things that I told him before, that this was duality of command, the introduction of parallel lines in command. Specifically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, you've told us that already. Mr. Lukic, are you interested to know what orders, when, where, what about? Okay. Let's ask. Could you give us one of these orders: Given where, when, and what about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can just speak of one. I cannot recall the places, times, and objectives as for others. But, for instance, on the 3rd of August, 1995, Karadzic; Krajisnik; the minister of defence, Ninkovic; the chief of state security, Krnajic [phoen], stopped by at my staff, and also Karadzic's advisor, General Subotic. Karadzic started about speaking renaming the Main Staff into the General Staff. I asked him -- actually, I asked him whether all of those present should be listening, and he said that everybody else should leave expect for Krajisnik, and then he said to me, General, we are renaming the Main Staff into the General Staff. General Mladic will be replaced and he will be the special advisor for defence for Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serb Krajina. And I shot back by way of a response saying that I would not be head of that General Staff. Krajisnik added, Radovan, let him be now. This is an initial action on the spur of the moment. As a soldier, he will have to receive his orders. The order did arrive the next day. Again, I refused it even in writing; that is to say, all generals of Republika Srpska refused and signed a petition to the Assembly of Republika Srpska. It was the Assembly that appointed Ratko Mladic as head of the Main Staff, so it is only the Assembly that can relieve him of that duty, not the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just intervene here for the sake of the correct transcript. The witness didn't say the "president" but he said the "Supreme Commander."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least that's what you heard. It will be verified. But the president was the supreme commander. We do agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is the same person only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, yes. No different, but Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a different term, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, what did you say? It was only the assembly that could replace and not the president, or did you say it could only have been the assembly, not the Supreme Commander, if you remember at all what it was? It's the same person, of course.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't remember whether I said Supreme Commander or president. But I know for sure that I mentioned the name of Radovan Karadzic irrespective of which term I used and his dual role is something that everyone is well aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Was there a clash, a conflict between General Ratko Mladic and the president, the Supreme Commander, Radovan Karadzic; and, if so, what did it consist of, and from when did it date? Could you tell us in a few sentences?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the war and especially after the war, there was a lot of talk about that. However, I never saw the two of them quarrel, and I never was present during anything like that. That there was this conflict is something that I first of from Ms. Biljana Plavsic on Saint Vitus Day, the 28th of June, 1993. A class of soldiers was being sworn in on that occasion, and she delivered a speech to them. And she started saying that the Supreme Command could not take General Mladic and she turned to me, addressed me, in front of these masses, and she said, General, I ask you to protect General Mladic. I tried somehow to caution her about that but that did not go. However, when she said that, there were 10.000 people there, parents, relatives of the young soldiers, and there was applause all round.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the next sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between Mladic and Karadzic there were other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said, "... there were 10.000 people, parents, relatives of the young soldiers," and there was -- and then the interpreters got lost. Could you repeat what you said after "parents, relatives of the young soldiers, and ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: What we can see in the transcript was "applause all round." But then another sentence followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you said "applause all round," and then you added something. Could you repeat what you then added after you said "applause all round."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried by way of a grimace to caution Biljana Plavsic and to indicate to her that this was not the place to discuss that. However, she went on, and I think that after referring to the applause I said that I never saw or heard the two of them quarrelling or squabbling. I attended sessions of the supreme command when the two of them exchanged views in a tone that was a bit sharper, also in terms of content, but I think that that is normal dialogue of two -- of the two most responsible people in the army. So it never looked like a quarrel to me. As for an open misunderstanding, not between General Ratko Mladic and Supreme Commander Karadzic, that happened at the 50th Session of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska on 15th and 16th of June -- I'm sorry, April, 1995. Karadzic and all deputies of the SDS rejected Mladic's expose about the situation and the needs of the VRS. That was made public, and I know that on the following day, in order to have a shock absorber of this, if you will, the two of them toured the positions of the 30th Division, the 1st Krajina Corps on Mount Vlasic. And then that was recorded, pictures were taken, it was filmed, and so on. So it was mitigated a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm -- put your next question to the witness, and please focussed. The witness gives very lengthy answers and they have got often to do something far away with the question. Please keep focussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, now I'm going to ask you something about the situation in the Army of Republika Srpska, and we can provide short and concise answers with regard to that. Is it true that the VRS had a shortage of fuel and in which periods was this most pronounced, if that was the case at all?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the war, we had fuel shortages. We were using the ammunition reserves that we had inherited from the JNA, and our materiel resources went down from day to day. This culminate before the assembly in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a shortage of manpower in the VRS? You can answer.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to establishment of VRS, we did not have a shortage of soldiers. We, however, had a lack of officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The sanctions that Yugoslavia imposed against Republika Srpska, how did they affect the situation in terms of the combat readiness of the VRS. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I see that I can go ahead. The sanctions that were imposed on the 4th of August, 1994, well, I personally expected a catastrophe. However, these were sanctions of the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or, rather, the government of Serbia. However, these were not sanctions of the people of Serbia. One of the measures included in these sanctions was, for example, prohibiting politicians and generals of Republika Srpska to cross the Drina river. Any time I had to cross the Drina river I would cross it without any problems whatsoever at the border; that is to say that the persons who were implementing this decision did not observe this decision of their government. This national patriotism was at work among the Serbs on the other side of the Drina. However, sanctions caused moral problems in the commands of the Army of Republika Srpska in the Main Staff, in the corps commands, because, until then, we always thought that we had a support in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, regardless of what happened. However, we lost that support after rejecting the plan of the contact group. Especially when sanctions were imposed in real terms on paper, we lost this one and only ally that had positive thoughts at least about us, if nothing else. However, when we realised that the behaviour of the people in Serbia was quite different from the behaviour of the government, we calmed down and we continued the war. Sorry, may I just conclude? So the imposition of sanctions by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia against Republika Srpska did not decrease the combat readiness of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the balance of power in Bosnia and Herzegovina? How was it affected by supplying the Muslim and Croat side with weapons? Also pressures by NATO?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the beginning of the war, our army was always on the losing end as regards the balance of power. First of all, the Muslims had Croats as their ally, then Croatia as ally. So not to go into the actually balance, 4:1, 5:1, I can talk about specific operations. For example, Operation Storm, 11:1 in manpower, 23:1 in equipment in that particular operation. So every cannon, every piece of equipment that crossed the border of Bosnia-Herzegovina went to the Muslim/Croat coalition, not to the Serbs. So it's only natural that we lost our power, and if you look at our warfare, you will see that in the second half of the war, we strove for victory, in particular, directions so that we would keep up the morale of the army and the people, like the counter-attack in Bihac and right now I cannot remember, Spreca. That is to say, small-scale operations that have to be efficient, though, in order to keep up combat morale. I will just give you one example: On the 31st of August, 1994, the Muslim Supreme Command issued a public statement, saying that in the fighting until then, during 29 months of war, they lost 235.627 soldiers. My conclusion when I heard that was that they were trying to justify NATO air-strikes against the Serbs that started on the 29th of August. And the question is: How big their army was if they had that kind of losses, a quarter of a million people. Eight per cent are world norms not -- or standards. Not to go into that now. We'd have to be talking about the Chinese army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately three minutes, the question started by the affect by supplying the Muslim and Croat side with weapons. I've not heard any specific reference to apart from all the weapons that entered into Bosnia and pressure by NATO. I've heard about who tried to influence NATO. But we are far away from the questions. Mr. Lukic, you should keep in control of the examination of the witness. And please keep that in mind by both putting clear, concise questions, and by interrupting the witness if he moves away from what you asked him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, it's not clear yet. You said that 23:1 was the ratio in terms of equipment. In whose favour in this operation that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Croat armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Main Staff was undermanned throughout as well? It was manned by 33 per cent. That's the information I have. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the war, 36 per cent was the highest level of manning reached. That was a conscious policy on the part of the head of the Main Staff so that as many officers as possible would be on the front line to command units, to lead units; whereas we, in the staff, took care of staff work and usually one man would be doing two or three related jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now briefly about units attached to the staff. You mentioned the 10th Sabotage Detachment, the 65th Regiment, and so on. When they were sent to the front line, is it correct that, at the same time, they would be resubordinated to the commander who would be heading that particular operation or action, or did people from the Main Staff command them in those situations when they would be sent into combat?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the operation in question was not a complex one - in other words, if not more than one or two corps were included - then parts of those units were resubordinated, such as battalions. Seldom did it happen that entire regiments or guards brigade would be subordinated. However, if it was a complex operation headed by either the commander of the Main Staff or myself, then that unit was placed under our command; that is to say, under the command of someone from the Main Staff. So the corps did not command the Protection Regiment which would be included in their operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the corps only commanded parts of units, if they had been resubordinated; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But resubordination is always limited, in terms of time and space. It has a beginning and an end, as well as two points in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned the equipment which remained in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is it true that in the territory controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council, there were still warehouses of the former JNA? And, if you know, can you tell us which warehouses remained in their territory?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that there were some, but I can't name any single warehouse in the territory of the Federation. I wasn't there during the war or in peacetime. But I do know what was left behind was the ammunition factory called Igman near Konjic and a cartridge factory which was taken from us in Gorazde called Pobeda. So they could continue producing ammunition for the needs of the coalition armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are nearing the end. Let me ask you something about General Mladic next. We know that following the meeting at which General Zivanovic had his going away party, or farewell party, you went to the west again. It was sometime after the 20th of July, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the 23rd of July, 1995. I know because that afternoon I returned to the western part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General Mladic, too, arrived in the western front - correct? - in August?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in early August.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the western front, did you discuss with him any events concerning Srebrenica in July, or were you busy with something else?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not discuss Srebrenica with him because I was busy preparing a session of the Supreme Command, which took place on the 1st of August, I believe. Later, events became more turbulent. On the 4th of August, Knin fell; on the 5th, Petrinja fell. Croats went further afield with Operation Storm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was focussed on whether you discussed Srebrenica or whether you were busy with other things. I don't think that Mr. Lukic would like to know exactly what other things you were busy with. He was primarily interested in whether you discussed Srebrenica. The answer has been given. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I am interested in it and I'm sorry if it wasn't reflected in my question. Save for Knin and Petrinja, which other municipalities fell during that period and what was it that kept you busy? You may begin answering.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot enumerate them all, but during that time, between the 1st of August and the Supreme Command session, following that date, 11 municipalities in western Krajina fell, starting with Glamoc, and there was another municipality which fell the same day as Glamoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it Grahovo?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It fell in the morning, and that day I evacuated people from Glamoc, so it wasn't lost in combat. Then there were other municipalities which fell one after another. Even before the 1st of August, before Croats arrived in Knin, Drvar had been bombed. So it was Drvar that fell, then Petrovac, then Kljuc, and all the way up to the Ugar river. Eleven municipalities in total. So I didn't care much to talk to General Mladic or to discuss Srebrenica at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did General Mladic ever tell you that he was in any way involved in the killing of prisoners in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for your other colleagues from the Main Staff or in terms of other possible sources in Republika Srpska, did you ever hear from any of those that General Mladic was involved in either capturing or killing of those prisoners in Srebrenica? You may answer.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did General Ratko Mladic order you to have the people in Srebrenica killed?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Order me?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, they have not even discussed it. Why -- it's -- it goes without saying, I would say, that the whole context of the testimony of this witness, that it's a totally superfluous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We had a base for this question in the questions from the Prosecution side, in direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did the Prosecution claim in any of the questions that Mr. Mladic would have ordered General Milovanovic to kill people in Srebrenica? Mr. Groome, is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I certainly don't recall saying anything -- anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither do I. But, if so, please take us to it, because we may have missed something, Mr. Lukic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just need two or three more minutes so maybe I should continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then you're invited to conclude your cross-examination in the next five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We heard what General Mladic said on the 12th of May, 1992, when he contributed to the discussion in -- following Kalenic's statement when he cautioned the politicians against engaging in genocide. Could you conclude at any point in time that General Mladic changed his position during the war? Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Until I went to the west in late October, General Mladic had not changed his position in terms of waging war or his position vis-a-vis the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was to be my next question, or at least part of it. Did General Mladic during the war ever order to have civilians or captured enemy soldiers tortured, to the best of your knowledge, or killed?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did hear on Radio Sarajevo a statement made by General Mladic. All of Bosnia-Herzegovina could hear it at the beginning of the war that the Presidency building is to be targeted to stretch out the Muslims. Another thing which I heard was a conversation in jest between him and Colonel Balac. Balac was sent to the environs of Srebrenica where he established communication with the Main Staff or the other way around. I don't know who called whom, but Tolimir, General Mladic and I were in the office, as well as someone else, perhaps. When General Mladic, through laughter, asked Balac, Klaso, are there any Turks there? - Klaso meaning because of the fact that they were in the same generation at the academy - he answered, Yes, there are as many as ants. And Mr. Mladic laughed and he said, Fire at them. And then -- then somebody in the office started waving at General Mladic to be careful what he was saying over communication lines --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness repeat the very end of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the very last part of your answer. We have on the transcript that somebody started waving at General Mladic to be careful what he was saying over communication lines. What did you then say following that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Tolimir tugged at his sleeve. He was upset, telling him, Watch your mouth. We are probably being listened to. And later on, we did find out that the telephone conversation between the two of them was indeed intercepted, although I don't know which armed force did, whether it was UNPROFOR or the Croats. It was broadcast on a Radio Sarajevo for several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did General Ratko Mladic order you anything, ever, which you believed that was unlawful and contrary to the laws and customs of war? Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you ever present when he ordered someone else to do something that would be unlawful and contrary to the laws and customs of war? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, in a few sentences, what kind and man and general was General Ratko Mladic? And that would be my last question.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can put it all in one sentence. During my service with General Mladic, he was a charismatic person, a giant with a soft heart, meaning that he did not hold things against people for long. He was a just and fair commander. He protected his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does that conclude your answer?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this concludes my questions, General. Thank you for answering them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. We'll take a break. But before doing that, Mr. Groome, could you tell us how much time you would need to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think about -- approximately 45 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately 45 minutes. Then you may already follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and we resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, you'll now be re-examined by Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, General Milovanovic. All the questions I'm going to ask you this morning are going to be very precise and focussed. Could I ask you to limit your answers to the precise piece of information that I'm seeking. Yesterday at transcript 17088 to 89, Mr. Lukic asserted to you that: "No one from the army could make decisions as to whether a convoy would pass through or not." And you replied, "Yes." I want to explore that answer in a bit more detail. Now, when we speak of convoys am I correct that there were two categories of convoys, the first carrying humanitarian assistance into the enclaves; and the second, convoys resupplying the UNPROFOR troops stationed in the enclaves; is that correct? You can answer whenever you're ready.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now with respect to the commission that Mr. Lukic inquired about yesterday, the -- the commission of the RS government that only dealt with humanitarian convoys, it had nothing to do with the UNPROFOR resupply convoys; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a committee for co-operation with foreign intermediaries in the war. Primarily, UNPROFOR, UNHCR, et cetera. Within that committee, there was a commission for the delivery of humanitarian aid. It was that commission which took decisions. The army did not take any decisions. It was supposed only to make way for the convoy, and the issues that I detailed yesterday. As for UNPROFOR resupply convoys, likewise the UNPROFOR commander would go through that particular committee. We only received information that an UNPROFOR convoy would take such and such a route, at such and such a time, and these convoys were checked just as humanitarian convoys were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now Exhibit P2222 is a chart of your comments regarding the convoys. And in item 3 of that chart, you identify Colonel Milos Djurdjic as the member of the Main Staff on this commission or committee. Am I correct that the Main Staff was represented on this commission?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, the witness made a distinction between the committee and the commission. In your last question you did put them together again. Commission being within the committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. And just so the Chamber knows why in yesterday's question and answer it was the word "commission" that was being used to refer to this body. So it may be a nuance in the translation. But I believe it's clear what we're speaking about -- the people who dealt with these convoys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, is it not the case that, despite the existence of a committee, which included a Main Staff officer, that the final say on whether a humanitarian convoy was allowed to proceed was -- was made by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the commission was formed, yes. But not after it was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I want to read you a question and answer from the Tolimir case and ask you whether it causes you to reconsider that answer. It's evidence that was taken on the 17th of May, 2011, at transcript page 14213. The question put to you by Mr. McCloskey was: "Who had final control? The commission or Mladic? "A. Final control was in the hands of the army, Mladic at check-points." Do you remember giving that answer and does that affect your answer today?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember and the answer given then does not affect in any way the answer I gave a moment ago. You read out to me the term "final control," which is the control of UNPROFOR at check-points, whereas, your previous question had to do with a decision and who had the final say, Mladic or the committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If the commission said that a convoy should proceed and Mladic said that the convoy should not proceed, would the convoys proceed into the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know because I did not experience such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now turn back to directive 7/1. It's your evidence this week that Mladic rescinded the portion of the order in directive 7 that you identified as being unlawful by not including the text in directive 7/1. My first question, in this regard, is whether Karadzic ever complained that Mladic had dropped a portion of Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, yesterday after the transcript recorded you as saying that directive 7 was not mentioned in directive 7/1, the Chamber drew your attention to two passages where it was. Having in mind those two passages, would that be an indication that Mladic intended directive 7/1 to be read in conjunction with directive 7?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the items where General Mladic refers back to directive 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, if a directive or order refers to another directive or order, would I be correct that the subordinate receiving that document would have the responsibility of reviewing the earlier directive or order?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that P1470 be brought to our screens. This is directive 7/1. And could I ask that we go to 3, page 3 in the original, and 4 in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On 3, can I draw your attention to the bottom of the page; and, in the English it's the full -- the first full paragraph at the top of the page. Now, General, this paragraph is composed of a single, long sentence. Am I correct in understanding that from this sentence that we can see that the Sadejstvo 95 operation included operations around Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not clear about the question, really. Was it: Do I agree with this or -- can you help me with it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. The question is: Does Sadejstvo 95 include military operations in the area of Srebrenica and Zepa, according to this?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Nowhere is Srebrenica mentioned, and I am not familiar with Operation Sadejstvo co-ordinated action 95. I heard about the operation in another case, but it was not within my sights when I was at the Bihac front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to the bottom two lines in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps if the usher could assist us by focussing in on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it well. There's no need to zoom in on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is it not clear from a plain reading of this document that Operation Sadejstvo 95 includes operations - and I'm quoting - "around Srebrenica-Zepa and Gorazde enclaves."

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. Those are the last words in that paragraph. So it does include activity around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in referring to this operation, Mladic states: "By carrying out planned combat battles and operations in accordance with directive number 7." Is this not a clear reference to the planned operations in accordance with directive number 7?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So do you agree with me that the phrase that you identified in directive 7 as being unlawful has been incorporated into 7/1, by reference?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said, speaking to you, I believe, that the Supreme Command acted inappropriately by sending directive 7 to second-level units instead of sending it to the Main Staff only and the Main Staff would then adapted it for the purposes of subordinate units. Subordinate units would, in that case, on the basis of Mladic's directive, rather than Karadzic's, be drafting their own orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But, General, you just told us that a subordinate would have the responsibility of looking at the documents referred to in an order or directive. Wouldn't a person, an officer, reading this sentence from directive 7, wouldn't they go back and look at directive 7 to find out what were the planned combat battles and operations that are in accord with directive number 7 [sic]?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, are we to understand that at line 20, page 29, where you first referred to "directive 7," you want to say "directive 7/1."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Much obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, may I repeat the question so there's no confusion. I misspoke. Given what you've told us about the responsibility of a subordinate to go back and look at the earlier order or directive that's referred to, wouldn't an officer, reading Mladic's statement here, or order here, in directive 7/1, wouldn't they be obliged to go back to directive 7 and within this sentence refer them to the order you said was illegal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may answer the question, Witness. You always may answer the question when it's clear that Mr. Groome has finished it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still stand by this, the distribution of directive 7 was inappropriately carried out by the Supreme Commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not the question. The question was whether someone reading the reference in directive 7.1 to directive 7 would have to look at directive 7 in order that to be fully able to implement directive 7.1. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And my next question is: Wouldn't this line from Mladic's order in 7.1, by carrying out planned combat battles and operations in accordance with directive 7, isn't that a specific reference to the line of directive 7 that you testified the day before yesterday was unlawful?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us what other planned operations in directive 7 this could be a reference to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't reproduce directive 7 off the top of my head now, but we will avoid any confusion by saying that the author of directive 7/1, that's to say General Mladic, aimed at cutting his directive short because these details are already contained in directive 7. In order for him to provide an assignment to subordinate units that would be clear and precise, he said something that is normally used also by you lawyers, pursuant to item such and such, to article such, of such and such a law. And those who are reading the text are then obliged to go back to that article or law that is cited and see what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that P1468 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's an order for defence and active operations, operative number 7, dated 20 March 1995 issued by Major-General Milenko Zivanovic, who was at this time commander of the Drina Corps. So that there is no confusion regarding the chronology, directive 7 was issued on the 8th of March, 1995, and transmitted by General Milovanovic on 17th of March. P1468 is an order by Zivanovic dated the 20th of March, P1470. Directive 7/1, was signed by Mladic on the 31st of March. Now, General, in your testimony at page 16996, you referred to an order in which Zivanovic copied the illegal phrase from directive 7. Can I ask that we go to page 3 of the original and page 5 of the translation. And if I can draw your attention to section 2, the tasks of the Drina Corps. And now if we turn to the next page of the translation, we can see that Zivanovic writes: "By planned and well thought out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." Is this the passage that you were referring to in your evidence the last couple of days?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, according to your evidence, this order issued by Zivanovic would be contrary to the wishes of the commander. Are you aware of any order communicated to Zivanovic that, after 7.1 came out, this particular passage in this order targeting the civilian population should have been rescinded? Is there any explicit order to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be found in Karadzic's directive 7. Zivanovic copied this from the original, which is directive 7. You yourself mentioned chronology. The corps received Karadzic's directive sometime on the 17th or 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think that everyone here is clear of the chronology. So my simple question to you is, is that this order came out before 7.1. Once 7.1 came out, was there ever an explicit order to Zivanovic to withdraw this order that he had issued to his subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that P1465 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is an order dated the 2nd of July, 1995, issued by the same Major-General Milenko Zivanovic. Now, General, this order is several months after the issuance of directive 7/1. Can I draw your attention to item 2 in this order, and it can be found on 2 in the original and 3 in the translation. The section starts with the phrase: "The command of the Drina Corps, pursuant to operations directive number 7 and 7/1 of the Main Staff of the VRS." My first question to you is: Does this indicate that Zivanovic's understanding of the relationship between directives 7 and 7/1 were that they were -- they both remained in effect and must be considered in conjunction with each other?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on this because I don't know what Zivanovic had on his mind when he was writing this. He referred to both directives, but I don't know which one he gives precedence to. And under the command system, it was directive 7/1 that he should have given preference to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, this -- the plain language of this document doesn't give preference to either. They're treated equally, are they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that, but I stand by what I said; that's to say, Zivanovic should have given a preference or primacy to Mladic's directive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And on what basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I say that on the basis of military subordination within the system of VRS where certain authorities cannot be sidestepped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it sidestepping if Mr. Mladic himself refers to directive 7 in the directives 7/1 he issued? That's not sidestepping. I mean, Mr. Mladic gave it its place in 7/1. So, therefore, it's not entirely clear to me what you mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fact that General Mladic refers to directive 7, Karadzic's directive, does not constitute any sidestepping of authority because Karadzic sent the directive to Mladic for implementation. Now it was up to Mladic to determine how he would convey this on to the units. And I did say that my previous evidence that Zivanovic made the mistake of not waiting for Mladic's directive but drafting his order for the defence effort on the basis of Karadzic's directive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, again before I read you a passage of this let's keep in mind that this document, this order, is several months after Mladic's directive 7/1 and specifically references the two. So if we can go to item 4 on page 2 in the original and 3 the translation. Halfway down that paragraph, after the word "objective," we read: "By a surprise attack to separate and reduce in size the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves to improve the tactical position of the forces in the depth of the area, and to create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves." Would it be a fair interpretation of this sentence that Zivanovic understood that both the separation of Srebrenica and Zepa and the removal of the civilian population from those enclaves, as indicated in directive 7, were still in effect?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may be mistaken. But in none of the directives, either 7 or 7/1, did I see the term "eliminate the enclaves." Nor can it be found in the transcription of tasks - that's item 2 - where Zivanovic lists the tasks of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you read the sentence that starts: "... by surprise attack, to separate and reduce ..." Can you read that sentence for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Objective: By a surprise attack fully separate and reduce in size the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, improve the tactical position of the forces in the depth of the area, and create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So I don't understand your evidence. Is your evidence that this is not related to directive 7 and 7/1 and that it's something that Zivanovic has done on his own accord?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And so it's your evidence that his reference to "elimination of the enclaves" is substantively different than directive 7's order: "By planned and well thought out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." My question to you is: If that situation is created -- create a situation of no hope for further survival or life in the enclaves, how is that different than the elimination of the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the following way: The order issuing authority in directive 7, that is to say, Karadzic, makes it incumbent upon the army to create conditions of unbearability and Zivanovic spells that out in concrete terms, says: Creates conditions for the elimination of enclaves; that is to say Karadzic did not say why life conditions should be made more difficult. That is understandable, presumably. And Zivanovic thought that it meant elimination of enclaves and that's what he wrote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I think the witness has now been given large opportunities not to testify about facts but about the interpretation of documents which is the primary task of the Chamber. Again, we have not stopped it, but ... there's one or more -- one or two more questions fine. But let's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- stay with this forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we please go to the last page on both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And General, when that comes up on your screen, can I draw your attention to the type written text directly under Zivanovic's name. It reads: "Typed in two copies and delivered to: 1. Original in the archive of the Drina Corps Command; 2. Main Staff of the VRS." Does this indicate that Zivanovic sent a copy of this to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does this mean that the Main Staff approved this order?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot conclude that on the basis of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to a portion of an interview that you gave on the 24th of August, 2009, in which this very document was discussed. On this topic, on this particular document, you were asked what it means, this endorsement. Your response was: "Original to archives, Drina Corps Command. You are right. Number 2, Main Staff of Republika Srpska. That means that it's probably been approved by the Main Staff." Do you recall expressing that with respect to this document back in 2009?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall, but I stand by what you said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it is your evidence today that this order of Zivanovic was sent to the Main Staff and approved by ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you left out the word "probably" and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- therefore, could you please put the question again to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is it your evidence today that this order was probably sent to the Main Staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was probably approved, that's at least what you read to us. Mr. Groome would like to know whether your evidence is that the reference to the Main Staff of the VRS means that the order is -- probably been approved by the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My final statement, if you will, shall be as follows: From this document, I see that the document was sent to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. But I do not know what the reaction of the commander of the Main Staff was, whether he approved it, whether he did not approve it. I cannot see that from this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. But apparently in your previous interview -- or could you say, Unless there is a response by the Main Staff that they disapprove it, that sending it and subsequent silence on the matter would mean that it is approved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not necessarily. However, it is not impossible that General Mladic and Zivanovic spoke and that he gave him approval in that way, just orally. Now whether Zivanovic wrote that down somewhere, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A simple question: If Mr. Mladic would not -- if the Main Staff would not have approved and if Mr. Mladic would not have approved, what would he have done in order to express such disapproval, under normal circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He would have stopped the order, and he would have given his own amendments, changes, et cetera. So he'd order, Zivanovic, change such and such a thing in such and such a way, and Zivanovic would be duty-bound to do that and to send it to General Mladic again with those corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, is there anything to your knowledge that this action was taken; that is, stopping the order and giving his own amendments, changes, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I was on the other end of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you may ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, yesterday at transcript page 17003 in response between -- in response to a question put to you by Judge Fluegge regarding directive 7, you said: "No. I saw this directive for the first time in the Tribunal building sometime around the 29th of May." What year were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm correcting the date and place when I first saw this. I saw this directive, that is to say its top and the end, on the 18th of October, 2005, in Banja Luka. It was shown to me by Prosecutor Peter McCloskey. I saw it again during my testimony on that 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is it also your evidence or your belief that General Mladic did not see directive 7 before Karadzic issued it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I don't know. But I do know that General Mladic appointed General Miletic to form the directive. So he must have seen that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, if I might just ask. Mr. Milovanovic, you were asked by Mr. Groome what year of the 29th of May were you referring to. You have still not given that. Could you please give us that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2007 is the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, if it were to be that Miletic did not consult either you or General Mladic about the contents of this directive, would that have been a breach of the principles of command and control that you've given evidence about during your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said yesterday that I would have consulted everybody in the Main Staff had I been in Miletic's shoes. Now whether Miletic did consult someone, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that 17473A be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I'm going ask you to look at each page. The text is very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I nevertheless go back to the previous question, Mr. Groome. The question was whether -- if Miletic would not have consulted either you or General Mladic about the contents, whether that would have been a breach of the principles of command and control. Your answer was: I would have consulted everyone. Whether Miletic did consult someone, you do not know. Do I understand that Miletic was under a duty to consult with Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how Miletic behaved. I've said several times already that I would have consulted both Mladic and the entire staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you have done that because you considered it your duty to do that under the system of command and control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Miletic was your direct subordinate. Did you ever reprimand him for having done this?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because I did not have an opportunity. I told you when I was first in contact with this directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I now ask that 65 ter 17473A be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, again, General, this is a relatively short document. I'm going to -- when you've had a chance to look at this page, please indicate that, and we'll advance to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Next page, please. I'm not terribly interested in the handwritten text.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Next one. General, having looked at these, does this refresh your recollection that on the 17th of March, you not only transmitted directive 7 to the 1st Krajina Corps but to the Drina Corps, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and the Herzegovina Corps? I've asked Investigator Yarmah to be present in court with the originals if you should care to see them.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need for the originals. But these documents that you showed me just now dispelled my dilemma about that document that we discussed yesterday. It only went to the 1st Krajina Corps. So I thought that with the regular sending to the other corps that that was -- that the head of office forgot. However, now, I see that it was sent to all the corps on -- at the same time. My signature is there. However, in relation to what I said yesterday, I can just say the following: The directive went simultaneously to all the corps and we see in the documents that they sent back when they received it. We saw that one of them received it on the 18th. And then the Herzegovina Corps, there is no confirmation on the document when he received it. I mean, there is no stamp of the head of office of the Herzegovina Corps. So I don't know when they received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we return to page 1. Are you referring to the endorsement by Zivanovic returning a signed copy of your transmittal letter, as instructed in the letter itself? And it's at the bottom of that page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But something is strange here now. I sent this on the 17th of March, 1995, via courier. And, ah, this is the 18th of March. I thought that it was the 18th of September. That's what it said. So he received it on the following day. Now I cannot remember the date when he issued his combat order. You did refer to the chronology. I think it was the 23rd?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It was the 20th of March. But that's not the focus of this particular inquiry. What I want to ask you is: In each of the four transmittal letters signed by you that we've now seen the fact that you're attaching a directive is clearly marked on the document; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, the day before yesterday, you defined a directive for us and you said that at transcript page 16974. You said: "A directive in war time is the highest form of doctrinally ordering or directing the activities of any military, including ours." General, is it really your evidence that you, as the deputy commander of the army, someone expected to take command of the army in Mladic's absence, is it really your evidence that you did not read the directive?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not read the directive. The directives were packed in envelopes. And on the envelope, it said, directive number 7 of the Supreme Command of the Army of Republika Srpska. Since I was in the Main Staff in passing, I happened to be there. I didn't read it. I stand by that. I've told you when I first came in contact with that directive. I read it in greater detail when I testified in May and June 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, then can I ask you, you've testified a few minutes ago that it is the obligation of a subordinate, when he receives a directive of an order that refers to an earlier one, is the obligation of that subordinate to go back and review that. When you read 7/1 and saw that it referred to directive 7, why did you not at that point go and read directive 7?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw directive 7/1 at the time when I saw directive 7, within the indictment of General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it -- it's your evidence today that as the deputy commander of the VRS, you did not have sight of two directives prior to the date -- I think you -- in 2005. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now switch to some evidence that Mr. Lukic dealt with today regarding Sarajevo. And in answer to a question of his, you described the -- the ultimatum by -- from NATO to withdraw artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter 09714 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It is order issued by General Milovanovic on the 9th of February, 1992 [sic]. General, this order is issued -- I'm sorry. This order is issued via teleprinter. Once you have a chance to look at it, can I ask you to confirm that, in fact, it is an order of yours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You think you said "1992," Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I take it you wanted to refer to "1994."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So my first question is: Do you recall issuing this order. Let me know when I can ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do I fairly characterise this document by saying when faced with the ultimatum, you issued an order for inoperable weapons to be moved into Sarajevo so that they would be the ones that were moved back in compliance with the ultimatum. Would that be a fair characterisation of this?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because I pointed out for as long as ultimatum-based threats of bombing are still on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders 09714 as well the previous exhibit, 65 ter 17473A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 17473A receives number P2248, and document 09714 receives number P2249, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2248 and P2249 are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I only have a few more questions for you. Today at the temporary transcript page 21, Mr. Lukic asked you: "Did General Mladic during the war ever order to have civilians or captured enemy soldiers tortured, to the best of your knowledge, or killed?" Your answer was, "No."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask 65 ter 10635 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is a memoire written by General Milovanovic called: "My View of the War in Bosnia: 1992 to 1995." General, when you see the first page of the document, can you tell us is it, in fact, the document I've just described?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was the work material for my book that is now called: "Truths and Delusions Concerning the War in Bosnia: 1992 to 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When did you write this book?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we now go to page 37 in both versions of the document, and in the translation I would draw the Chamber to the last few lines of the first full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise, General Milovanovic, I'm not sure exactly where the passage is in the original, but I will read the passage I am interested in and you'll hear in the translation: "The Muslim Supreme Command had ordered them to tie up our troops so that we could not come to the aid of those of our forces fighting against a major Muslim offensive in Sarajevo which had started on 16 June 1995. The response of the VRS to these raids by the Muslims led to the tragic events in Srebrenica, where the Serbian forces did some things that they should not have done and for which there had been no military justification." My question is simply: Do you still stand behind this passage?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is my analytical approach to the problem after the war, ten years after Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do intend to -- no, actually I've read that into the transcript. There's no need to tender that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, my last exhibit that I'm going to ask you to comment on is a portion of an interview that you gave on the 7th and 8th of July, 2009. The transcript can be found at 65 ter 30269B. And when that's up on the screen, I'm going to ask Ms. Stewart to play the audio, and I'd ask you to listen carefully. I do want General Milovanovic to be able to hear his voice, so perhaps if we could not have translation and just rely on the transcript, and if that could be played again, if that's suitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that the transcript be put up on the screen so that the General has the benefit of seeing the written text.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, was that, in fact, your voice that we just listened to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At the end you said: "He came in and took over the command from Krstic. He was the one to come in Srebrenica and it happened to him, what happened." "... happened to him, what happened," were you referring to the massacre of the men in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is stated explicitly here that I said "it happened to him." So whatever fate befell him is -- was something of his own doing. He ended up indicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. We are already a bit late for the break. Mr. Lukic, how much time would you need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll consult with my colleagues and the client. If any, very short, very few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because if it's a matter of one or two minutes, we could consider to take those few minutes now. If it's more, we should take the break --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please consult.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We obviously are waiting for my response, only I do not know what I have to respond to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was how much time you would need, if any at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will have to go through the re-direct to [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... so you need the break to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take the break first.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I simply tender the last exhibit, 30269B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The excerpt of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to clarify in that. At this moment I don't have the audio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
