utterances.text: You don't have the audio. Could we reserve a number and already have the transcript under that number and MFI it until we have the audio.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Document 30269B receives number P2250.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. I asked to this, Mr. Groome, that where you earlier referred to P2222, that is not yet admitted. It is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milovanovic, we take a break. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, could you give us any further indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's zero seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Zero seconds. Then Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to 65 ter 30269B, Ms. Stewart has provided the Registrar with a copy of the audio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar had informed me about that. Which means that the audio, now having been added - Mr. Lukic, I heard of no -- I think there were no objections - P2250 is therefore now admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, the Defence has just informed the Chamber that there are no further questions for you, which means that this -- your testimony is concluded. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for answering all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You're excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While the next witness is to be prepared to be stand by, I'd like to deliver a decision of the Chamber. It is a decision on the Prosecution's motion to add Witness RM183 to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter witness list. On the 12th of July, 2013, the Prosecution filed a motion for leave to add Witness RM183 to its Rule 65 ter list. The Prosecution submits that the motion should be considered in light of its 20th of June, 2013, notice of its intention to reduce the evidence it adduces in support of its case. Given the decrease in total number of witnesses and live witnesses resulting from the notice and the motion, the Prosecution states that the Defence will require less preparation time and will not be prejudiced such benefits constituting good cause to add the witness to its Rule 65 ter witness list and demonstrating that the addition is in the interests of justice. On the 26th of July, the Defence filed its response objecting to the motion in its entirety, based on the Prosecution not justifying its late amendment to its Rule 65 ter witness list, its lack of showing good cause, the proposed mode of testimony and the potential impact on the fairness of the trial. The Chamber recalls and refers to the applicable law concerning amendments to the Prosecution' Rule 65 ter witness list as set out in its previous decision filed on the 22nd of August, 2013. At the outset, the Chamber notes that the Defence's objections regarding the mode of testimony through which Witness RM183 will eventually testify are premature and misplaced. Instead, the proper forum for such arguments would be in response to a motion tendering the evidence. Accordingly, those parts of the response dealing with the proposed mode of testimony will not be further considered in this decision. The Chamber considers that the witness's evidence is prima facia relevant and of probative value with regard to good cause the Chamber considers that the Prosecution has not shown good cause to add the witness to its Rule 65 ter witness list at this stage. However, the Chamber finds that addition of the witness will result in a limited additional burden for the Defence, in particular, given that the witness's evidence deals with issues that have been raised with other witnesses. In this respect, the Chamber has also considered that the Prosecution proposes to tender the witness's evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis through a motion which is still to be filed. Should the Defence require additional time to respond to such a motion, the Chamber will consider such a request. In light of the aforementioned, the Chamber finds that it's in the interests of justice to allow the addition of Witness RM183 to the Prosecution's 65 ter witness list, and this concludes the Chamber's decision. If the witness is ready he can be escorted into the courtroom. Unless there are any preliminary -- any other matters to be raised before we do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. In fact in speaking with Mr. Stojanovic, we hope to conclude this witness's testimony today as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That ... .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Soja. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Soja, you'll first be examined by Ms. Hochhauser. Ms. Hochhauser is counsel for the Prosecution. You find her to your right. You may proceed, Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And good afternoon to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Can you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: My name is Milomir Soja.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Mr. Soja, you gave a statement to the ICTY dated 24 July 2004, and also testified in the trials of Dragomir Milosevic and Radovan Karadzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If I could please have 65 ter 30264 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Soja, when you're able to see something on the monitor in front of you, can you tell us, please, is that the statement that you gave to the ICTY in 2004?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And have you had the opportunity to review this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Can you confirm that it is both accurate and truthful?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Have you also had the opportunity to listen to the audiotape of your testimony from the Dragomir Milosevic case in your own language?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And can you confirm that that is also both accurate and truthful?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: In regard to both the 2004 statement, that's now on the screen, and your prior testimony from the Dragomir Milosevic case, can you tell the Chamber whether, if asked the same questions today, you would provide, in substance, the same information that you provided in that statement and prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, with that, I tender 65 ter 30264 which is the statement as well as 30265, which is a selection of relevant transcript from the Dragomir Milosevic case, along with one associated exhibit which is a drawing prepared by Mr. Soja which has the 65 ter number 28333.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First the 2004 statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30264 receives number P2251.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and with the testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30265 receives number P2252.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And one associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28333 receives number P2253, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2251, P2252, and P2253 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might proceed to a brief summary of the witness's evidence for the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so and I take it that you have explained to the witness what the purpose of it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes. He is aware. The witness is an electrical engineer. Before the outbreak of the war, he was employed by Energoinvest in its power electronics department. He was mobilised at the outbreak of the war in 1992. And after his release from the armed forces in December of 1994, he took up his work obligation in the company Energoinvest Automatika in Ilidza. In the spring of 1995, Mr. Soja and one of his colleagues were asked to go to the Pretis ammunition factory in Vogosca, Sarajevo, regarding the modification of the ignition system for an air-bomb launcher. They were accompanied by an officer from the Ilidza Brigade of the VRS. At Pretis, Mr. Soja met Major Krsmanovic, an officer of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Krsmanovic told the witness that at that time that in addition to the launcher of the Ilidza Brigade, there were two functional air-bomb launchers, one in Vogosca and the other in Ilijas. Mr. Soja subsequently learned that the SRK also had an air-bomb launcher in Blazuj. And in case I've mispronounced that it's B-l-a-z-u-j. Mr Soja reports that Major Krsmanovic was opposed to the electronic modification of the launchers since this would have rendered the equipment less reliable. However, the witness was asked to perform modifications using electronic components as the Ilidza Brigade intended to use this new system on their air-bomb launcher. Twice the witness attended to malfunctioning modified air-bomb launchers out in the field. On the second occasion in the summer of 1995, the witness was requested to attend the launching of an air-bomb, targeting the cold storage plant in Stup from a launcher positioned close to the witness's workplace. The first attempted launch failed. That same evening, the witness observed the launch of the air-bomb from a distance of about 150 metres. The air-bomb did not reach the cold storage plant but exploded prematurely on the territory under the control of the VRS. During the relevant time, Mr. Soja heard the launching and detonation of air-bombs about five to six times. And his evidence states that there is a characteristic sound connecting with their launching and detonation. Your Honours, that concludes my summary. I have two very brief areas of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If I could please have 65 ter 09119 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And as its coming up, I'll ask you, Mr. Soja, in your prior testimony of what is now exhibit number P2252, beginning at the bottom of e-court page 8 and into e-court page 9, you discuss how you learned of the existence of modified air-bomb launchers in positions in Vogosca, Ilijas, Ilidza and Blazuj. Can you tell us, looking at 09119, which is now on the screen, and discusses the issuance of aerial bombs from the Pretis factories. Do the brigades and commands listed therein comport with your knowledge of the positions of modified air-bomb launchers in and around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: The Ilidza Brigade, that figure tallies. With the Ilijas Brigade it has to do with Blazuj. With the Igman Brigade the number is fine. Although items 2 and 3 is something I'm not exactly aware of, I don't know what it pertains to, so items 2 and 3 I'm not certain which brigades those are.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: But items 1, 4, and 5 are consistent with the locations you discuss in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Yes, based on what I could hear from the people I came in contact with concerning the launchers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, the Igman Brigade covers the Blazuj launcher that you were -- that you talked about; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours I would tender 65 ter 09119, at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 09119 receives number P2254, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If I could please have 65 ter 03826 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, sir, as it's coming up, I'll ask you, you are familiar with the mechanical elements of the modified air-bomb and launcher production. Can you tell us about the materials listed here. Were these typical of those used in the production of the launchers that you saw?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: The materiel on the left were the mechanical components that could be used for a launcher. The list on the right-hand side has to do with the electrical components.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And the electrical components, are those also consistent with what you knew of the launchers that you saw?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: The launcher I saw had a completely different type of electronics of its ignition system than shown here. But such elements as the cables and starter, all those could be used to devise electrical ignition of the launcher which used aerial bombs.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And to be -- the devising the electrical components of the launcher is in fact the task that you were asked to work on in that time-period; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: In the factory I worked, where I was under work obligation, we had a different solution to this. We used different electrical -- electronic components. In principle, it may well be the same but we went about it another way. These are classical standard electrical components whereas we relied on electronics more.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 03826 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 03826 receives number P2255, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness? Mr. Soja, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will try to conclude my examination by the end of the day today, and let us try to be as focussed as possible. Can we have Exhibit P2251 in e-court. Page 2 in the B/C/S and in the English version of the witness's statement. Let us focus on the last paragraph of item 2. My question has to do with clarifying something in this part of your statement. You say that while you served your military term with the JNA in Slovenia, in Ribnica, you were trained to operate a multiple rocket-launcher. Please tell us what kind of training it was and what kind of skills and knowledge did you acquire in terms of this weapon's precision and use, since you were trained as marksman?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: In Ribnica, I was assigned to the unit of multi-rocket-launchers, the so-called VBRs. I was there on secondment from the sabotage unit. I was trained as a gunner of the 120-millimetre rocket-launcher. It was a standard asset that JNA units had. I cannot recall any specific details which had to do with the weapon's precision, but the weapon did have its standard characteristics such as range, sights, procedures, and everything else that was prescribed for such standard assets. It also had appropriate precision. I can't say that at distances of 5 kilometres, it could hit a target with an error of minus or plus 5 metres. That's something I can't say any longer. But we underwent the kind of training as planned and envisaged within the units of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am waiting for the transcript - do not hold it against me - so that we have everything in the transcript. In the same document, let us look at page 3, the last paragraph in the B/C/S. In the English version, it is also page 3, item 4, paragraph 4. You say that sometime in the spring of 1995, from Risto Ceranic, your company's manager, you were notified that some work had to be done on an aerial bomb launcher that was to be produced at Ilidza for the needs of the Ilidza Brigade and you make reference to the Pretis factory. Let me ask you this first: Can you provide us with any more detail in terms of when it happened in the spring of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: I really can't recall anything precisely when it was that spring. Let's say in early spring. I really can't recall the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because of one incident in our indictment. Was it before May 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: It is possible that it was before May. I think it was before May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mention the Pretis factory. Let me ask you this: In terms of your knowledge about the Pretis factory, do you know that even before the war it was one of the largest factories for special-purpose production in the former SFRY. It was a factory where the rocket projectiles for the Orkan-type multiple rocket-launcher was produced and also FAB-100 and -250 aerial booms were produced there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: The Pretis was a well-known factory in the former Yugoslavia. It was a large one. It was best known as a car factory. It was also well-known that all large factories in the former Yugoslavia had at least a department each tasked with special-purpose production for the needs of the JNA. To tell you the truth, I didn't know what the Pretis was included in. What I did know was that they produced larger-calibre ammunition, shells, in principle, rather than standard ammunition. But I can't be any more specific than that. I don't know which shells precisely they produced or whether they produced the aerial bombs of this kind. It is possible, because they did produce larger-calibre shells, at least according to what I could hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to your statement, you were received - you and your work-mate - by someone by the last name of Krsmanovic. And you referred to it on page 4 in both versions of your statement. Apparently it was your impression that he was the most senior in terms of rank of the people involved in the project concerning aerial bombs. Let me ask you this: Can you tell us anything in more detail, if you have any knowledge, as to who Mr. Krsmanovic is?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Krsmanovic twice in my life. The first time was when we came to see what kind of requests they had in order to create our variant of electrical launching system of aerial bombs. The second time was when I attended a failed bomb launch which was supposed to target the cold storage facility at Stup. As far as I recall, he had the rank of major, and I have no other information about him. There was no one to ask, and I didn't hear any such information. I simply have no other information, save for what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because I'm interested in the following: In any testimony thus far, were there any indications in your statement which would show that it was an officer of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Based on my impression and based on what I could see, I concluded that he was an active-duty officer. I simply had no other knowledge, either back then or now. Now, whether he was an active officer with the SRK or whether he had come from Yugoslavia to perform some specific tasks, that's something I don't know. I think he was an active-duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At which point did you see the launcher in real life, as well as a modified aerial bomb?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: I saw the launcher for the first time in the Energoinvest factory, where the mechanical segment of the launcher was being manufactured at the same time as the electronic part that we were producing. I must say that I had no idea that in this factory, Energoinvest, which was an adjacent facility, something of the sort was being produced. That was when I saw the launcher for the first time. As for the modified aerial bomb, I saw it probably when I went out for an intervention, and I was also able to see it when this failed launching of the bomb took place aimed at the cold storage place in Stup.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was charged with designing and manufacturing the launcher that you were referring to in Energoinvest?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: I don't know who the constructor of the mechanical segment of the launcher was. What I do know is that it was finally made in a factory called Tat [phoen], which is a well-known factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time was the launcher already on a mobile platform or was it still on the plant floor, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: The launcher was mounted on a -- a truck that was parked in the factory. That was when I saw it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you help us with the technical components of it? The aerial bomb would have rocket motors fitted on it, right, and they would be the ones who would set the bomb in motion. Is my reasoning correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: If you mean to say that the rocket motors are fitted onto the rear body of an aerial bomb, then you're right. Onto the rear of the body of an aerial bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us this: Where exactly were these rocket motors fitted onto the rear part of the aerial bomb?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: The aerial bomb that I saw on this particular occasion already had rocket motors or engines fitted on to it. Where this was done, I don't know, but quite possibly it could have taken place in the Pretis factory. They were quite capable of doing this sort of job. The area where I was at the time, well, it brings to mind Pretis, as the most plausible candidate for such a job in this area that was under the control of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that in order for such a projectile to be manufactured a multi-disciplinary approach was required. There had to be electrical engineers, people versed in mechanical engineer, et cetera, in order to come up with such a type of projectile?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could I briefly take you back to one of your previous questions. You asked where exactly were these rocket motors fitted onto the rear part of the aerial bomb? I understood that, but I may be wrong, that you asked where exactly those motors would be attached to the bomb, or is that mis-understood. Yes, because the witness did not answer that question. The witness did answer another question. That is, in what factory, in what work-shop, et cetera, was this done, and that's, of course, a totally different question from the one which I understood you to ask the witness. I just put it on the record. If you are satisfied with the other answer, not to your question, then please proceed, if you want to receive the answer please put the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe I received an answer to my question. Since I -- my -- my -- my question -- the initial question was whether it was the rear part of the bomb where the rocket engines were fitted, and I got an answer to that question already at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness told us that it was fitted on the rear part. And then, I think, you then asked him where exactly they -- on the rear part they were fitted. Now, if you are satisfied with the answer that it was on the rear part, then there was no need to put the question, because I think the witness had answered that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If you'll allow me to, I will eliminate this ambiguity from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you heard this. Can you tell us which part of the body of the aerial bomb were the rocket engines fitted onto?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: The rocket engines were attached to the posterior part, or the rear part, of the bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you this: If my understanding is correct, there were two occasions when you were in person able to see these modified air-bombs.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Yes, two times.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you, on both of these occasions, able to see how many rocket engines were attached to the rear part of the air-bomb?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: There were three rocket engines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because of a document I'll use later. Did you, at any point, hear, if not see, that there were modified aerial bombs with four rocket engines?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: I heard that there were bombs with a single rocket engine. Were there ones with more? Well, I'm sure there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let me ask you this in a technical sense. The design and the part of job as you, as an engineer, had to allow for the ignition of which engine or engines?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Well, we first had to make it possible for the fuse of the bomb to be armed, and then for the ignition of the engine -- engines. So the segment we were working on covered both these issues. First, we had to make sure that the fuse would be armed; and then electricity had to reach certain points of the rocket engine, from which the rocket engines would be ignited.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Technically speaking, did it also imply the ignition of all the three rocket engines attached to the rear part of the aerial bomb at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: These rockets, anti-hail rockets, that were supposed to counter hail storms and that were supposed to get ignited all at once, where were they obtained from?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: In conversation with Major Krsmanovic, whom we mentioned earlier, I heard that what was being used as rocket engines to ignite these aerial bombs were -- that it was actually rocket engines used as anti-hail rockets. And I heard that this came from Serbia. I don't know if there was a plant in Bosnia-Herzegovina that produced such rocket engines. Perhaps there was one, but I didn't hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you agree with me that at least in these two cases that you yourself witnessed, these were ordinary anti-hail rockets, original anti-hail rockets of the Grad type?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: I was told that these were anti-hail rockets but I wasn't able to -- or anti-grad rockets, but I did not see them and I did not hear of anyone producing makeshift rocket engines so it had to be a standard industry product.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that it may involve the Grad rocket type, called G-r-a-d, which also means hail incidentally in B/C/S. We're not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on your training and experience such a rocket engine industrially produced would have had to go through the usual process of testing before it -- it is sent out onto the market?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: At any rate, the rocket engines, including the ones used to counter hail storms, had to go through certain testing before being put to use. Anti-hail rockets are used in civilian situations. What I mean to say is that the civilians would be the ones operating them so they had to be standard engines and rockets used in countering hail storms nowadays. At any rate, I think it's the same system that is being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just remind you of this. I'd rather that we not go into the document again. You were shown a document detailing electronic parts that were used by the manufacturer, and you said that this wasn't something that you normally used in your line of work. My question is this: Would such electrical parts be in the function of -- or in the service of igniting an engine of the anti-hail rockets, just as these engines were fitted onto the bombs that you were able to see?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, the principle and the objective are the same, but the road taken to reach that objective was different from the technical standards that you applied and the people who were requesting the supply of that material there.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Yes. Those were classical electrical components. Whereas, we used electronic components. But the principle is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Another technical question before we move onto documents. We were also told that such an anti-hail rocket engine would be able to lift the weight of a FAB-100. So I'd like to ask you this: Based on your expertise, can confirm for us that such an engine would be able to lift and set in motion such a bomb weighing 100 kilograms?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: I don't have any specific knowledge of the characteristics of these engines, but I did hear that the smaller bombs only had a single engine. I did say that previously, that this was something I heard. I have no knowledge, but I suppose that it's possible. If three engines can lift a bomb that is two and a half times heavier then I'm sure a single one would be able to lift a lighter bomb, a bomb as light as this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps we should now take the break if we plan to work until 2.15, and I do believe that we will complete the examination of the witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you still need, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have four documents left and three photographs. No more than 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would then leave at least ten more minutes for either re-examination or questions from the Bench. We take the break, and we first ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we will resume at a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please -- oh, we already have it in e-court. So I don't need to call up another document. P2251, page 4 B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please help us with this, sir, and could you explain an answer that you provided here. You say: "During the summer of 1995," Your Honours, I am reading chapter 5, the third paragraph, "I heard a number of times a characteristic sound of the air-bombs flying in the area. For the first time when I was at home in Osijek, next time when I was in Stup. I also heard this sound later but cannot remember where I was then." Can you tell us, to the best of your recollection, how many times did you have the opportunity of hearing this characteristic sound?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly how many times I cannot be precise, but five, six, or about ten times. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this was, which time-period, which year? When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: That was roughly the beginning of the summer, when that last fierce fighting took place around Sarajevo. Roughly in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to ask you. The sound that you heard, does that correspond to the time of intensive combat activity during the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now please take a look at the next paragraph of your statement. You say: "I do not know if air-bombs were used against civilian objects." Now I'm going to ask you whether, at any point in time, you had any knowledge as to the objectives or, rather, the targets at which these projectiles were fired?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: As I've already said, I heard this characteristic sound several times. It had to do with the flight of an air-bomb. However, I know directly of this one case, when I was present during this failed attempt to fire, and later on I was relatively nearby in Energoinvest when the bomb was launched towards the cold storage plant. And then there's this other case that everybody knows of, I think it was it was even the media, that one of these bombs hit the building of radio television. As for these other targets, I'm really not aware of the specific ones involved or, rather, the places where the bombs fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in view of your military involvement throughout these years of the war, can you tell us, can you -- or can you confirm for us whether the facility of the Simis factory, the cold storage plant, was the place from where the artillery of Bosnia-Herzegovina fired at the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: That plant was certainly used by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, what kind of weapons and artillery pieces were used for activity from there, I cannot confirm that. It is possible that there were artillery pieces there too, but it is certain that very often there was firing against -- against Ilidza and this other location where I spent the last year of the war in my work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to ask for P3. In e-court, that is page 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you to help us with this, because I assume that you are familiar with the terrain? This is a photograph that you had see a bit later. It is one of the three incidents from the indictment in this case, and it has to do with something that, according to the indictment happened on the 26th of May, 1995. Now this is what I'm asking you: In view of your place of residence, can you recognise this part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: I think that it is the neighbourhood opposite the radio television and close to the bus depot of the Sarajevo Bus Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that the facility to the left of this apartment building marked with a red circle, so this place with a red roof, is that the police station in that part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Also, in view of the fact that you possibly are familiar with this area, could you give us an estimate as to how far away this red circle is from the mentioned police station?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say exactly. Approximately it may be, say, about 100 metres. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: General guidance to the parties, distance are be to be measured rather than to be estimated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Together with the Prosecution, we are going to do that, as we did in two other situations. May I just clarify this with the witness, the place where the modified air-bomb fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us an estimate as to how far away the building of Radio TV Sarajevo is from the place where this projectile fell?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Well, it's roughly a couple of hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to ask that we look at P3, again, together. So it is P3. In e-court, it would be page 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask the witness -- Do you know where the projectile fell, or is it on the basis of the red circle that you gave your estimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of the red circle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Stojanovic, only the red circle covers at least 20, 30, if not more, metres. So, therefore, it doesn't really help. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due respect, this red circle is an agreed location on the basis of the testimony of other witnesses and we have the exact location of where the projectile fell. There is a document and the exact address of the place where the projectile fell. So, I believe, that there is going to be no dispute between us and the Prosecution with regard to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing I said is that the red circle, I take it, then, that the -- it's an agreed place where the projectile fell. But the projectile does not -- is not 40 metres long but is 1 or 2, or 3 metres. And, therefore, there is an inherent inaccuracy already by using a red circle rather than a very specific point to start your measurement. But let's proceed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could I now ask you, please, to take a look at this photograph as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is incident -- it is the incident that occurred on the 16th of June, 1995, and the location is the square of international friendship and that's the indictment reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know this part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Well, not in great detail but I know a bit, like any other part of Sarajevo. I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would be interested in the facility across this road that goes to Ilidza. The road is popularly known as Bitumenka. Do you see it in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is as follows: How far away was Bitumenka from the approximate location where the projectile fell, from this red circle?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Well, it's about 100 metres, or maybe a bit more, 100, 200 metres, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At any point in time, during the years of the war, did you know whether the area known as Bitumenka was also used for the needs of the Army of the Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: I did not know about the use of these areas, and let me not engage in guess-work. Now I do have an opinion of my own, but, no, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During your involvement, did you have any direct or indirect knowledge of such a modified weapon being tested?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: I heard from Mr. Krsmanovic that they tested one launcher on the hill of Zuc and that they had some problems then with these cables for firing, and probably that's why he mentioned that testing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge as to whether the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the summer of 1995, had the human resources and technical resources -- in view of all the persons that you had from before the war did they have the resources to make such a projectile?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: From the point of view of technical and human remain resources, I think they were certainly capable of making something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to conclude with the following question: In view of your training in the JNA and your professional education and training, can you tell us anything about the precision of such a weapon?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: I really have no information about its precision. What I do know for sure is that, on that launcher, there were some elements for targeting. That is to say, taking a particular position in terms of height and direction. So it was used for sighting. Now how close these bombs fell in respect of the desired target, that is something that I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see who it was that used these sighting devices on the mentioned launchers in those two cases when you were nearby? Were these professionals?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: The first time I was there, no one used it because we came there to repair a technical thing that went wrong. Second time I'm not sure. Possibly the bomb had already mounted on the launcher before it was in this position. But, at any rate, there was an appropriate team there that was in charge of this launcher. And they handled it. I, myself, do not remember seeing a man handling that part of the mechanism. I really have no such recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'm going finish with the following question. Did you have any information, at any point in time, that the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska was in any way involved in setting targets for the use of this modified weapon?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that. I personally do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give you an opportunity to put further questions, I would have a few questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you explain to us what the whole purpose of this exercise with these modified air-bombs was? Was it the huge explosive power in the body of the bomb, or was it a lack of other ammunition? Or was it -- why did they use such a rather complicated way of non-standardized production of projectiles? What was the purpose of it, instead of using the standard rockets through a standard rocket-launcher, or using other projectiles? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: This is my opinion in that regard. It is a fact that the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska at this point in time in the war were very poorly supplied with ammunition. That could have been one of the reasons. Now, the second possible reason - these are just my assumptions, that's what I'm telling you about now - is -- well, you said it was complicated. But, actually, it was a very simple way of hitting a target with an air-bomb, much simpler than doing it from an aircraft because you need an aircraft and specialised pilots, and so on and so forth, so this was a simple way of firing an air-bomb that, at any rate, was more destructive than standard shells. I assume that all of this led to the motivation for constructing this kind of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that it's more easy, perhaps, to fire it from the ground than to drop it from an aeroplane. But if you say they're more destructive than standard shells, that is, that it would cause more damage upon impact?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the one time you observed that a modified air-bomb was fired at the Simis cold storage facility, you said it landed in VRS-controlled territory. How far was that approximately from where the target was, the target being the Simis cold storage?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, the bomb did not fall and detonate, but, rather, exploded in mid air. The device that I was working and was actually put out of commission. It was no longer used in the development of the asset due to that failure and I have no further contact with the crew of that launcher. I never received any official information as to what had happened. As far as I know, as far as I heard, the bomb exploded in the air. It had not fallen. It exploded in mid air before reaching the cold storage facility. It never reached the target and for some reason detonated in mid air.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you told us that sometimes three propelling rockets were mounted on the modified air-bombs, sometimes more, sometimes one. You were specifically involved in the ignition mechanisms. Could you tell us whether the precision of the simultaneously igniting several propelling rockets mounted to such an aerial bomb, whether that would have any possible impact on the accuracy of the ballistics to be expected? That is, the trajectory you would expect the bomb to fly.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be -- would the ballistic characteristics, due to these technical issues, be better or worse than, I would say, normal projectiles, such as mortars or other standard produced projectiles?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: In any case, there was a problem to deal with, which was the simultaneously ignition of the rockets. If that problem is solved appropriately and adequately, then, in principle, the asset would be on a par, at the same level as the other artillery assets. As far as I know, with mortars too you have additional charges depending on the weight of the gun powder. It is that that determines the place where the shell will land. Any artillery weapon, in principle has potential difficulties with the system providing initial acceleration to the shell. In this case, specifically, it had to do with the simultaneous ignition of the rocket engines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was that problem resolved so that it really would -- that they would ignite all exactly at the same moment?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: As regards the solution I attempted to reach, we used ultra quick electronic starters to ignite the engines. As for standard solution, according to the material I saw a moment ago, and according to my knowledge, they relied on very simple solutions using simple starters, simple switches. All engines were connected to a single starter. Once contact is established, separate wiring is used to lead electrical impulses to all the engines at the same time. I don't think it amounted to a specific technical problem. The length of wiring was the same from the starter to the ignition mechanism, voltage is released simultaneously through the entire wiring system, and the rest was up to the characteristics of the specific engines, in terms whether they would, indeed, ignite at the same time or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If ignition would not be exactly at the same moment, could that influence the trajectory by creating a disbalanced propelling power?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: I have no experience and no knowledge so as to be able to speak about any time delays in the ignition of engines. Of course, the greatest problem would be if one or several engines failed to ignite completely. That could be a problem. However, I simply have no knowledge. If you bring the voltage simultaneously to the entire circuit, well, then I can't really say what sort of delay we could have in the different times of ignition in specific engines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Last question: Did I understand you well that you have no knowledge about the ballistic characteristics of these modified air-bombs with the propelling rockets mounted to them?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: If you have in mind precision and range, then, indeed, I have no knowledge as to that, in terms of this weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, I have no further questions. Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Just one.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: At page 77, line 23, in response to one of the Judge's questions just now, you -- regarding the simultaneous ignition and finding a solution, you said "as regards to the solution that I attempted to reach," and I just want to be clear, the solution that you attempted was never -- was never successful ; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: There may have been a misinterpretation. We did reach a solution, as for the problems in that solution had nothing do with the launching of the rocket. To put it expertly a comparator device was too sensitive which was involved in the process of arming the bomb and thus disabled the launch. The bomb was not launched in the first place. In order to perform a launch, as I mentioned at the beginning of my testimony, one needed to arm the fuse. If that failed the electronic system would not allow ignition. Such problems amounted to a failed launch such as the case when I was present. But I did come up with a solution.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: But, I guess, what I'm trying to ask is: Other than the failed launch that you witnessed, you're not aware -- are you aware of whether your solution was ever successfully utilised?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: The launcher, with my solution, definitely fired air-bombs with my device. It is just that such problems occurred too often, resulting in a disability to launch, and that is why the solution, as envisaged by me, was ultimately terminated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I do understand that you then returned to a rather simple electric system compared to a more complex electronic system you had -- you had drafted, you had ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The crew of the launcher, on the day of the failed launch, came to see us at the factory, and we produced appropriate cabling so that they could do it in the standard way with a switch and a battery, as I have explained a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, no further questions. This, then, concludes your testimony, Mr. Soja. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench and I wish you a safe return home again. You are excused. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: There is just one issue, and I can raise it more properly on Monday, if we're in a hurry to get out, about the adjudicated fact that was redacted on page 4, an unredaction of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If would you not mind we would do that on Monday, because we have taken already -- we've stolen already, six -- six or seven minutes from those who are assisting us. We adjourn until Monday, the 23rd of September, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 23rd day of September, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.23 p.m.,
